pm13.notes: Accurate and fully cited. Padded with unrequested bullets on flared needle jets, plugging and scaling, roughly doubling the needed length.
pm13.answer:
Look at the stream. If the jet breaks up and disperses right at the nozzle, the nozzle is worn and should be replaced. A good nozzle gives a laminar (solid) zone before the water breaks up, and a worn one has a very short laminar zone [DOC a1b709c1-b90f-4687-ad80-b9fb21515901 p.3].

- **Self-purging nozzles:** These are the exception. Their two-piece orifice means the flow starts breaking up as it leaves the nozzle even when new, so this test doesn't apply to them [DOC a1b709c1-b90f-4687-ad80-b9fb21515901 p.3].
- **Flared needle jets:** A flaring needle jet is another sign of a worn or damaged nozzle. It shows up in felt moisture and permeability scans, damages the felt cap, and doesn't clean contaminants off the surface [DOC 39e95278-beb1-4937-867a-db98ca39f611 p.19].
- **Plugged nozzles:** A plugged fan nozzle looks different from a worn one. Check fan nozzles daily for plugging, and check the spray quality of hard-to-see nozzles at each shutdown [DOC a1b709c1-b90f-4687-ad80-b9fb21515901 p.12].
- **Scaling:** Scaling from hard water also plugs nozzles, so watch the spray pattern [DOC a1b709c1-b90f-4687-ad80-b9fb21515901 p.12].

pm15.notes: Misses internal starch for stiffness and light calender sizing of the top liner. The pulping-lines section is unrequested and the answer runs ~179 words, over the limit. The ratio estimate is properly labelled as general knowledge.
pm15.answer:
The library doesn't give a base-to-top weight split for two-ply kraft linerboard, so I can't quote a ratio from a source.

What it does say is how the two plies differ:
- **Base (bottom) liner:** high-yield kraft pulp, cooked to 55–60% yield. It is refined out of the blow tank, washed, then given an extra "de-shive" refining step [DOC 30d870b7-8b32-475a-9f65-e8f3bd87bd7b p.1].
- **Top liner:** a lower-yield, well-refined unbleached kraft, cooked to about 48–50% yield. The top liner is chosen for appearance and printability. Some mills use bleached kraft when a cleaner, brighter look is specified [DOC 30d870b7-8b32-475a-9f65-e8f3bd87bd7b p.1].
- **Separate pulping lines:** the most common system uses two complete kraft lines, one for each ply. Top-liner screen rejects usually go to the base line so the top liner stays exceptionally clean [DOC 30d870b7-8b32-475a-9f65-e8f3bd87bd7b p.1].

The library has no source for the ratio itself. From general engineering knowledge: the top liner is usually the thinner ply, roughly 15–30% of total basis weight, with the base ply making up the rest. Check this against your own mill's furnish and grade specs.

pm14.notes: All points correct and cited. 207 words against about 150, with unrequested floating-disc, fibre-development and capacity-limit paragraphs. These sections pad the answer.
pm14.answer:
Most mills choose disc refiners because they cost less to buy and run. Smook lists these advantages over conical refiners [DOC 01a335fe-bfba-4f11-b32c-df2de03d8521 p.1]:

- **Lower no-load energy use.** The benefit grows as energy costs rise.
- **Higher consistency.** They can run at higher stock consistency.
- **Higher loading and speed.** They can take both.
- **More versatile plate design.**
- **Self-correcting wear.** High and low spots mate evenly. In conical refiners they don't.
- **Smaller footprint.**
- **Lower capital cost per ton of production.**

The two-sided floating-disc design adds two more. Pressure is equal on both faces, so the disc centres itself and the refining energy splits equally between the two sides. The axial thrust forces balance, so no thrust bearing is needed [DOC 01a335fe-bfba-4f11-b32c-df2de03d8521 p.1].

Fibre development is not the reason. At the same operating conditions, conical and disc refiners develop fibres in a similar way [DOC 01a335fe-bfba-4f11-b32c-df2de03d8521 p.1]. Smook also describes disc refiners as the more recent type, with many designs, and says they offer significant advantages over the older conical refiners [DOC d9815fa5-40a2-474b-9932-eaf665991fc0 p.30].

Discs have one limit. Maximum rotation speed depends on disc diameter, which limits capacity. Sunds added a conical section at the disc periphery to get around this [DOC 01a335fe-bfba-4f11-b32c-df2de03d8521 p.3].

pm16.notes: Does not distinguish SEL (intensity) from specific energy (amount of refining, kWh/t). The final result comes after the definition, and the closing manual-example line repeats the result.
pm16.answer:
Specific edge load (SEL), also called refining intensity, is the net refining power divided by the length of bar edge crossings per second. It is expressed in watt-seconds per metre (Ws/m). Higher SEL gives more fibre cutting and shortening. Lower SEL gives more fibrillation. [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.23] [DOC 856ff3f6-9be4-42e7-b4dc-fee63dfd3cfd p.34]

Your refiner works out to about 1.2 Ws/m.

The formula is SEL = Net kW / (Bar Edge Length × Motor Speed × 1 min / 60 s). [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.41]

Net power is the motor load minus the no-load power. [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.23]

Calculation:
- Speed: 600 rpm ÷ 60 = 10 rev/s.
- Edge crossings: 30 km/rev × 10 rev/s = 300 km/s = 300,000 m/s.
- SEL = 363,000 W ÷ 300,000 m/s = 1.21 Ws/m, which rounds to 1.2 Ws/m.

The AFT manual works the same example (363 kW, 30 km/rev, 600 rpm) and also gets 1.2 Ws/m. [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.41]

pm17.notes: Misses the reduced-diameter plate savings (30-150 hp, e.g. 46 to 40 in saves about 150 hp). At 280 words it is padded with the full NL formula and the intensity formula, which were not asked for.
pm17.answer:
Rotor speed and plate diameter drive refiner no-load power most. Plate pattern and wear also matter. It matters because only the power above no-load changes the fibre.

**What drives it**
- No-load is the power used to pump and viscously shear the fluid. It is mostly set by rotor diameter and rotational speed, and the bar and groove pattern can also affect it significantly [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.32].
- Speed: it scales with the cube of rotational speed. Active plate diameter enters at the power 4.3 [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.33].
- Pattern: groove depth and the hydraulic section ratio (groove width over bar plus groove width) have a dramatic effect [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.33]. The calculation is NL = 102 × (RPM/100)³ × (Da/100)^4.3 × (2Gw/(Bw+Gw)) × (Gd/4), with NL in horsepower [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.33].
- Wear: no-load is highest with new plates and can be 60–80% lower when they are fully worn [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.32].
- Flow rate, consistency and plate gap have only a minor influence. Rotating mass has no effect on no-load. It only affects start-up acceleration and torsional loads [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.32].

**Why it matters**
- Net power applied to the fibre is total motor power minus no-load [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.32].
- Refining intensity is calculated from that net power: I = (Applied Motor Power – No-Load) / [RPM × Bar Edge Length × (min/60s)] [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.23]. If no-load is wrong, specific energy and intensity are wrong.
- No-load energy produces no measurable change in the pulp [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.32]. It is pure energy loss, mostly at the disc periphery where speed is highest [DOC 01a335fe-bfba-4f11-b32c-df2de03d8521 p.3].

I did not check PM1's own refiner data for this answer.

ce13.answer:
The flow is about 2.24 ft³/s.

The TAPPI formula for a rectangular weir with end contractions is Q = 3.33 × (L – 0.2 × H) × H^1.5, with Q in ft³/s and L and H in ft [DOC 2324ca0e-e2cb-4ac4-8f6c-1c90e2a03701 p.4].

Q = 3.33 × (2 – 0.2 × 0.5) × 0.5^1.5 = 3.33 × 1.9 × 0.3536 ≈ 2.24 ft³/s

The ft³/s to gpm conversion isn't in the library. From general engineering knowledge, 2.24 ft³/s is about 1,000 gpm.

The source says L should be 4–8 times H [DOC 2324ca0e-e2cb-4ac4-8f6c-1c90e2a03701 p.4]. Here L/H = 4, so you are at the low edge of the valid range.

pm18.notes: 320 words, about double the ~150 limit; the long library-quote section pads the answer. General knowledge is clearly labelled. RCT caliper and operator sensitivity are not explicitly mentioned. McKee is not named.
pm18.answer:
**Short answer:** Both tests measure edgewise compression. SCT/STFI is generally the better predictor of box performance. The library has no source that directly ranks the two on box prediction. That ranking comes from general engineering knowledge, given below.

**What the library says**
- Ring crush (RCT) is the traditional method. A ½" × 6" strip is rolled into a cylinder about 2" in diameter and compressed axially between two plates. The maximum load is the result. [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.18]
- Short-span compression (STFI) has become more widely used in recent years. [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.18]
- The compression measurement is made over a very small region to prevent buckling. Failure occurs when the fiber wall collapses. [DOC 6e312421-09ec-48b8-97ec-a68bbff246e8 p.23]
- Edgewise compression is hard to measure properly because of bowing, buckling and crushing of the loaded edges. Results differ from method to method, and conversion factors are often lacking. [DOC 168553e0-baa3-4e06-827d-54415678796a p.57]
- One empirical cross-direction relationship over a wide range of linerboard weights is STFI = 1.436 × ring compression. [DOC 168553e0-baa3-4e06-827d-54415678796a p.57]
- RCT is considered to relate to the eventual compression strength of the combined board. [DOC c93229dc-2711-42b6-9211-821d0e0902e1 p.7]
- In one study, top-load box results were about 9% lower, which "apparently reflects" lower ring crush. [DOC 168553e0-baa3-4e06-827d-54415678796a p.36]

**General engineering knowledge (no library source)**
- In ring crush, the curved, unsupported strip can buckle or fail in a mixed mode. This is worse on heavier or lower-stiffness sheets, so RCT partly reflects bending stiffness and not just compressive strength.
- STFI clamps a very short span, about 0.7 mm. It therefore measures true in-plane compressive strength and avoids buckling.
- Box stacking strength follows edge crush (ECT) of the combined board. ECT depends on the liners' compressive strength, and STFI tracks that more directly.
- RCT is still useful as a cheap mill control test, but it is less reliable when furnish, basis weight or refining change.

ce14.notes: Accurate, with the slot width and vacuum factor cited to p5. The unrequested paragraph that rescales the source's 250-inch example adds length without changing the answer.
ce14.answer:
About 4,500–6,000 cfm per Uhle box. I assumed the 300" is the slot length across the machine, which the source doesn't state outright.

The source says slot area depends only on machine speed, and 2,500 fpm needs 1" of total slot width [DOC 56ec08f5-d829-4786-b810-b1a7de9c7f74 p.5]. It then multiplies that slot area by a vacuum factor of 15–20 cfm per in² [DOC 56ec08f5-d829-4786-b810-b1a7de9c7f74 p.5].

- Slot area = 300 in × 1 in = 300 in².
- Airflow = 300 in² × 15–20 cfm/in² = 4,500–6,000 cfm.

The source's own example is a 250" machine at 2,500 fpm, which it gives as 4,000–5,000 cfm per box [DOC 56ec08f5-d829-4786-b810-b1a7de9c7f74 p.5]. That range matches 16–20 cfm/in² rather than 15–20, since 250 × 15 would be 3,750. Scaling that example to 300" gives about 4,800–6,000 cfm. Use roughly 4,500–6,000 cfm to size the box, piping, separator and vacuum source [DOC 56ec08f5-d829-4786-b810-b1a7de9c7f74 p.5].

ce15.answer:
The pump needs about 52.5 hp of hydraulic power, or about 39 kW.

The TAPPI formula is hydraulic power (hp) = Q × H / 1714. Q is flow in gpm and H is the pump's differential pressure in psi [DOC 2324ca0e-e2cb-4ac4-8f6c-1c90e2a03701 p.3].

Calculation: 1,500 × 60 / 1714 = 90,000 / 1714 ≈ 52.5 hp.

Using 1 hp = 746 W [DOC 2324ca0e-e2cb-4ac4-8f6c-1c90e2a03701 p.18], that is 52.5 × 0.746 ≈ 39.2 kW.

This is the power delivered to the fluid. The shaft (brake) power the motor must supply is higher, because it also covers pump efficiency. For example, at 75% efficiency it would be about 70 hp. That efficiency is my own assumption, and the library gave no pump efficiency to use.

ce16.notes: Accurate and fully cited. At 175 words it runs over the 150-word limit, padded by the second-source formula, the geometry-term explanation and the plate-wear aside, none of which were asked for.
ce16.answer:
No-load power falls to about 51% of its current value, a drop of about 49%.

No-load power scales with the cube of rotational speed [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.33]. The AFT formula has NL = 102 × (RPM/100)³ × other terms [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.33]. The other terms are plate diameter and bar and groove geometry. The diameter term is Da^4.3, and the geometry terms are groove width, bar width and groove depth. These stay the same if you don't change the plates. A second source gives the same cubic dependence: No Load (kW) = (2.299×10⁻¹³)(Diam^4.249)(RPM³) [DOC 856ff3f6-9be4-42e7-b4dc-fee63dfd3cfd p.30].

Calculation: NL₂/NL₁ = (720/900)³ = 0.8³ = 0.512

The change is 1 − 0.512 = 0.488, which is a 48.8% reduction.

I have no absolute figure for this refiner. If you give me its current no-load kW, multiply it by 0.512 to get the new value.

The no-load figure also falls as plates wear, by as much as 60–80% from new to fully worn [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.32]. The actual number therefore depends on plate condition as well as speed.

ce18.notes: Calls the thermocompressor part of 'the cascade' rather than an alternative to it, so MUST 3 is missed. Citations are supported despite the key listing no source. At 231 words, the 'why mills use it' and memory notes are unrequested.
ce18.answer:
A thermocompressor is a steam-jet ejector. It uses high-pressure motive steam to pull in low-pressure blow-through and flash steam from a dryer group. It discharges the mixture at an intermediate pressure, and that steam goes back to heat the same group.

How it works:
- The cross-section has a body, a suction port for low-pressure steam, a high-pressure steam inlet, a spindle, a nozzle and a diffuser. The discharge is intermediate-pressure steam [DOC 212d6dd4-0711-4fdc-8e33-735d3a13d5de p.12].
- In the cascade, blow-through steam from the dryers is boosted by mixing with motive steam and reused, usually in the same section [DOC 212d6dd4-0711-4fdc-8e33-735d3a13d5de p.12].
- It also holds the differential pressure the dryer siphons need for drainage. The steam side must sit above the condensate side [DOC f2d6b892-8f3a-49f6-bfb1-8f6beada12e7 p.2]. Berlin says the group is "bathing in its own juice" [DOC f2d6b892-8f3a-49f6-bfb1-8f6beada12e7 p.29].

Why mills use it:
- Each section gets independent pressure control, and sections can be grouped freely [DOC 212d6dd4-0711-4fdc-8e33-735d3a13d5de p.12].
- It avoids the loss of electrical generation that would occur if the motive steam were used elsewhere [DOC 212d6dd4-0711-4fdc-8e33-735d3a13d5de p.12].

Limit: it only works if enough motive steam is available. Otherwise the amount of mixed steam is too big [DOC f2d6b892-8f3a-49f6-bfb1-8f6beada12e7 p.29].

The memory tool returned a permission error, so I answered from the library only. I did not check whether PM1 has a thermocompressor, or which dryer groups it serves.

ce17.notes: Gives the laminar limit as ~2,000 instead of ~2,300. The cited 'pumps like water up to 6%' passage sits awkwardly with the non-Newtonian plug-flow explanation. At 293 words it is about twice the needed length.
ce17.answer:
The library has no source for the Reynolds-number criterion itself, so the first part comes from general engineering knowledge. Two library passages cover pulp stock.

**Laminar or turbulent (general engineering knowledge, uncited):**
- Calculate the Reynolds number, Re = ρvD/μ = vD/ν. Here v is the mean velocity, D is the pipe diameter and μ is the viscosity.
- Below about 2,000 the flow is laminar. Above about 4,000 it is turbulent. Between the two it is transitional, and you should design as if it were turbulent.
- Laminar flow has a parabolic velocity profile, and friction loss rises linearly with velocity. Turbulent flow has a flatter profile, and friction loss rises roughly with velocity squared and depends on pipe roughness.

**How pulp stock differs:**
- The AFT refiner manual says stock at 2–6% consistency can be treated as an incompressible fluid with water-like properties. Pumping characteristics up to about 6% are essentially the same as water. [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.34]
- The same page says friction loss in pipe flow differs slightly with consistency and pulp type. [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.34]
- Smook says medium-consistency technology fluidizes suspensions up to 12% consistency so they behave like Newtonian fluids. [DOC 5964733d-306e-4207-a72d-c3ebb900a35e p.17] That implies stock above roughly 6% does not behave like water without fluidizing.

**More general knowledge, uncited:**
- Fibres form a network at higher consistency. Flow then runs as a plug, with a water annulus at the wall.
- Friction loss falls as velocity rises (shear-thinning behaviour) until the plug breaks up and the flow becomes turbulent. A plain Reynolds number based on water viscosity does not predict this.
- Stock-specific friction-loss charts or the vendor's method are therefore used instead.
- At low consistency, below about 1–2%, stock behaves close to water.

n09.notes: Accurate and fully cited, and the general-knowledge reasoning is clearly labelled. At 289 words it is nearly twice the knowledge limit, padded with C-factor, intensity-range, too-low-SEL and extra drainage bullets.
n09.answer:
**Specific edge load (SEL)** is the energy spent per unit length of bar crossing. It describes how hard each refining impact is, and is also called refining intensity [DOC 856ff3f6-9be4-42e7-b4dc-fee63dfd3cfd p.34]. It is usually expressed in watt-seconds per metre (Ws/m) [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.23].

**Calculation**
- Use net power, not motor power. Hydraulic losses (no-load power) heat the fluid without refining the fibre, so subtract them from the motor load [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.23].
- Formula: I = (Applied Motor Power – No-Load) / [RPM × Bar Edge Length × (min/60 s)] [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.23].
- Worked example: Net 363 kW ÷ (30 km/rev × 600 rpm ÷ 60 s) gives 1.2 Ws/m [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.41].
- SEL ignores fibre characteristics, so it is a benchmark. C-Factor analysis adds plate geometry [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.24].

**Why recycled fibre needs a lower SEL**
- The library states "Recycling requires lower SEL" but gives no recycled-fibre-specific reason [DOC 856ff3f6-9be4-42e7-b4dc-fee63dfd3cfd p.34].
- Higher SEL gives more shortened and cut fibres. Lower SEL gives more pronounced fibrillation [DOC 856ff3f6-9be4-42e7-b4dc-fee63dfd3cfd p.34].
- Intensity above the recommended range causes severe fibre cutting, plate clashing, short plate life and poor strength development [DOC 856ff3f6-9be4-42e7-b4dc-fee63dfd3cfd p.36].
- Fibre cutting slows drainage and lowers strength [DOC d9815fa5-40a2-474b-9932-eaf665991fc0 p.27]. Low-intensity refining gives more fibrillation, less cutting and better fibre development [DOC d9815fa5-40a2-474b-9932-eaf665991fc0 p.29].

The library has no source for this part; from general engineering knowledge: recycled fibre has already been dried and refined at least once, so it is shorter and more fragile. It has little length left to lose, and gentle, fibrillating refining is how you recover bonding strength without cutting it further.

Going too low has its own cost: poor fibre development and an inefficient freeness drop [DOC 856ff3f6-9be4-42e7-b4dc-fee63dfd3cfd p.36].

n10.notes: Never defines % original capacity as tested ÷ original capacity at the same speed and vacuum. The unrequested seal-water section and the extra TIP example add padding. Claims are accurate and all cited.
n10.answer:
About $18,000 a year is wasted.

Equation 3 gives the wasted energy cost as annual energy cost × (1 − % original capacity) [DOC a92ccac2-eca7-4b0a-a2cc-bd07d3da9fa5 p.4].

Calculation: $60,000 × (1 − 0.70) = $18,000 per year.

The reason is that a pump worn by erosion or corrosion keeps drawing the same horsepower and seal water as a new one [DOC a92ccac2-eca7-4b0a-a2cc-bd07d3da9fa5 p.3]. At 70% of original capacity, 30% of the energy buys no vacuum. The TIP's own example works the same way: an 86% pump wastes 14% of its power [DOC a92ccac2-eca7-4b0a-a2cc-bd07d3da9fa5 p.3].

The same formula applies to seal water cost (Equation 4), so the pump is also wasting about 30% of its seal water spend [DOC a92ccac2-eca7-4b0a-a2cc-bd07d3da9fa5 p.4].

The 70% figure should come from a test at the pump's optimum vacuum level, compared with the manufacturer's curve [DOC a92ccac2-eca7-4b0a-a2cc-bd07d3da9fa5 p.3].

n11.notes: Covers density and bonding, and all claims are cited. Misses three key points: fibre modulus and strength limit well-bonded sheets; stiff, thick hardwood fibres help and yield matters little at constant density; CD compressive need and orientation/drying-strain effects.
n11.answer:
Density mainly controls it. The library says linerboard compressive strength is set mainly by the factors that raise sheet density, which are wet pressing and refining (freeness).

- Compressive strength is "primarily affected by factors influencing density, such as pressing and refining." Tensile strength and modulus also depend on wood yield and species [DOC 168553e0-baa3-4e06-827d-54415678796a p.19].
- The same report's Table I ranks wet pressing first and freeness second for compressive strength [DOC 168553e0-baa3-4e06-827d-54415678796a p.20].
- Higher density increases compressive strength [DOC 168553e0-baa3-4e06-827d-54415678796a p.41].
- Compressive strength rises quickly with z-direction bond strength up to a critical level, then more slowly. High-consistency forming raises internal bond and compressive strength but lowers tensile strength [DOC 168553e0-baa3-4e06-827d-54415678796a p.20].
- The authors speculate that compressive strength is limited by bending and buckling of weakly bonded fibre layers [DOC 168553e0-baa3-4e06-827d-54415678796a p.20].

This is a 1982 Institute of Paper Chemistry survey [DOC 168553e0-baa3-4e06-827d-54415678796a p.35].

n12.notes: Accurate and fully cited, but padded at 219 words against a ~150 limit. Unrequested extras: the uhle box dwell-time paragraph (self-admittedly off-topic), the couch vacuum limit, and the PM1 disclaimer.
n12.answer:
A flatbox near the couch generally needs no more than five or six slots. The Doug Sweet paper says slot widths are usually reduced as the sheet approaches the couch [DOC 56ec08f5-d829-4786-b810-b1a7de9c7f74 p.4].

Other ways to reduce table drive load, from the same page:
- **Fewer flatboxes and less slot area.** Many tables have too many of both. Remove unneeded flatboxes and those with excessive slot area, and use higher vacuum near the wet/dry line, after formation is complete [DOC 56ec08f5-d829-4786-b810-b1a7de9c7f74 p.4].
- **Low-drag ceramic covers.** Rework flatbox covers with a material such as silicon nitride. Together with the changes above, this can easily save 10–20% of power across the couch, wire turning roll and other former drives [DOC 56ec08f5-d829-4786-b810-b1a7de9c7f74 p.4].
- **Accurate vacuum measurement and control on every element.** Also stay within the physical maximum vacuum limits of each element [DOC 56ec08f5-d829-4786-b810-b1a7de9c7f74 p.4].

The same paper says more dwell time (slot area) than the machine speed needs only adds vacuum pump capacity and power, with no benefit [DOC 56ec08f5-d829-4786-b810-b1a7de9c7f74 p.5]. It makes that point for uhle boxes, not flatboxes.

The couch has a limit on vacuum. Too much vacuum can mark the sheet, which is avoided by keeping solids high enough after the flatboxes [DOC 7d704e0a-0ca7-4284-8fb9-dc6721c03b8a p.12].

I did not check PM1's own flatbox configuration or drive loads.
